steps.label: Why Store Many Values Together?
steps.content:
Why Store Many Values Together?

A program often needs to work with many values of the same type, not just one.

  • An array stores a fixed number of values under one name.
  • Each value has its own position, called an index.
  • Cambridge pseudocode arrays start counting at position 1, not 0.
  • A loop is the natural way to work through every position in an array.

steps.label: Practise Tracing an Array
steps.content:
Practise Tracing an Array

Practise following a loop that works through an array one item at a time.

Steps

  1. Open Trace Tables.
  2. At the top of the page, select Cambridge pseudocode.
  3. Open Walkthrough and choose Array Iteration.
  4. Predict what the program will output before pressing Step Forward.
  5. Press Step Forward until every line has been traced.

Complete when: the table shows a row for every pass through the loop and the final output.

The task is to add up three test scores that are already stored in an array.

steps.label: Write It Yourself
steps.content:
Write It Yourself

Use the same structure you just learned, but write it yourself this time.

Task

The array Heights = [120, 135, 142, 128, 150] is already stored, five values. Write pseudocode that:

  • adds up every value in Heights
  • outputs the total

Remember

  • Set Total <- 0 before the loop.
  • Use FOR Index <- 1 TO 5 to visit every position.
  • Add each value to Total inside the loop.
  • Output Total after NEXT Index.

steps.label: Check Your Understanding
steps.content:
Check Your Understanding

Questions to ask around the room:

  • What does DECLARE create?
  • What position does a Cambridge pseudocode array start counting at?
  • What does FOR Index <- 1 TO 5 count through?
  • Why is a loop the natural way to work through an array?
  • What does NEXT do at the end of each pass?

steps.label: Plenary: Question 1
steps.content:
Plenary

Use everything from today. Try this on your own before checking your answer.

Task

The array Marks = [18, 25, 12, 30] is already stored, four values. Write pseudocode that:

  • adds up every value in Marks
  • outputs the total

Remember

  • Set Total <- 0 before the loop.
  • Marks has four values, so the loop must count from 1 to 4.
  • Output Total after NEXT Index.

steps.label: Plenary: Question 2
steps.content:
Plenary

Harder than Question 1, an IF inside the loop this time, not just a running total.

Task

The array Numbers = [5, 12, 8, 20, 3, 15] is already stored, six values. Write pseudocode that:

  • counts how many values in Numbers are greater than 10
  • outputs the count

Remember

  • Set Count <- 0 before the loop.
  • Numbers has six values, so the loop must count from 1 to 6.
  • Use an IF inside the loop to test each value.
  • Only add 1 to Count when the IF is true.
